questions.question: What is AWS Elastic Beanstalk?

options.text: A serverless compute service
A PaaS that automatically handles deployment, scaling, and health monitoring of web applications
A container orchestration service
A managed relational database service

explanation.correct: Elastic Beanstalk is a Platform as a Service (PaaS) — you upload code and it handles EC2, load balancing, auto scaling, and monitoring automatically.
explanation.why: A is Lambda, C is ECS/EKS, D is RDS.

questions.question: How much does AWS Elastic Beanstalk itself cost?

options.text: $0.01 per hour per environment
$5 per month flat fee
Nothing — it is free; you pay only for the underlying AWS resources
$0.10 per deployment

explanation.correct: Elastic Beanstalk has no additional charge. You only pay for the AWS resources it creates, such as EC2 instances and RDS databases.
explanation.why: This is a common exam trap — students assume there is a service fee, but there isn't.

questions.question: Which of the following programming languages is NOT supported by Elastic Beanstalk?

options.text: Java
Python
COBOL
Node.js

explanation.correct: COBOL is not a supported Elastic Beanstalk platform. Supported runtimes include Java, Python, .NET, Node.js, PHP, Ruby, Go, and Docker.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are all natively supported platforms.

questions.question: In Elastic Beanstalk, what is an 'Application'?

options.text: A running EC2 instance with your code installed
A logical container that holds all versions of your code and all environments
A CloudFormation stack
A single deployment of your web application

explanation.correct: An Application is a logical container — it holds application versions and environments. The actual running deployment lives in an Environment.
explanation.why: C is what Beanstalk uses internally, but from a user perspective the logical unit is the Application.

questions.question: In Elastic Beanstalk, what is an 'Environment'?

options.text: The programming language runtime chosen for the application
A named group of configuration settings
The actual running deployment — contains EC2, load balancer, auto scaling, and all provisioned resources
A version of application code stored in S3

explanation.correct: An Environment is the actual running deployment. It contains the EC2 instances, security groups, ELB, auto scaling, and all other resources needed to run your app.
explanation.why: Application versions are stored in S3 but that is an Application Version, not an Environment.

questions.question: What does Elastic Beanstalk use internally to provision all AWS resources?

options.text: AWS Systems Manager
AWS CloudFormation
AWS OpsWorks
AWS Config

explanation.correct: Elastic Beanstalk uses AWS CloudFormation under the hood to create and manage all the resources in your environment. You can see the CloudFormation stack in the console.
explanation.why: A is for configuration management, C is for Chef/Puppet automation, D is for compliance tracking.

questions.question: A company wants to deploy a Java web application on AWS without managing any infrastructure. Which service should they use?

options.text: Amazon EC2 with manual setup
AWS Lambda
AWS Elastic Beanstalk
Amazon EKS

explanation.correct: Elastic Beanstalk is designed exactly for this scenario — developers upload code and AWS handles all infrastructure provisioning and management.
explanation.why: EC2 requires manual setup, Lambda is for serverless functions not traditional web apps, EKS requires Kubernetes knowledge.

questions.question: How many environments can a single Elastic Beanstalk Application have?

options.text: Only one
Maximum two (Dev and Prod)
Multiple — there is no hard limit on the number of environments per application
Maximum five

explanation.correct: One Elastic Beanstalk Application can contain multiple environments. A typical setup might have Dev, Test/Staging, and Production all in the same application.
explanation.why: There is no prescribed limit — you can create as many environments as your use case requires (subject to AWS service limits).

questions.question: What environment type should you choose in Elastic Beanstalk to stay within the AWS Free Tier?

options.text: Load Balanced environment with t2.micro instances
Single Instance environment with a free-tier eligible instance type
Worker environment with default settings
Multi-container Docker environment

explanation.correct: A Single Instance environment with a t2.micro or t3.micro instance type is free tier eligible. A Load Balanced environment immediately creates an Elastic Load Balancer which is NOT free tier.
explanation.why: ELB costs approximately $0.008/hour — always choose Single Instance for learning/testing.

questions.question: Which AWS resource does Elastic Beanstalk NOT automatically delete when you terminate an environment?

options.text: EC2 instances
Security groups created by Beanstalk
S3 buckets used to store code versions and logs
Elastic IP addresses

explanation.correct: S3 buckets created by Elastic Beanstalk are NOT automatically deleted when you terminate an environment. You must manually empty and delete them to avoid ongoing storage charges.
explanation.why: EC2, security groups, and EIPs are all terminated/released when the environment is deleted.

questions.question: What health status color in Elastic Beanstalk indicates that your application is unavailable or critically degraded?

options.text: Yellow
Grey
Blue
Red

explanation.correct: Red (Degraded/Severe) indicates the application is unavailable or experiencing critical errors. Yellow is a warning state. Grey means no health data (environment is pending/launching).
explanation.why: Green = Ok, Yellow = Warning, Red = Severe/Degraded, Grey = Pending/No data.

questions.question: By default, how often does Elastic Beanstalk collect CloudWatch monitoring metrics?

options.text: Every 1 minute
Every 5 minutes
Every 15 minutes
Every hour

explanation.correct: By default, Elastic Beanstalk collects CloudWatch metrics every 5 minutes. You can enable enhanced health reporting for more frequent (1-minute) monitoring, which has an additional cost.
explanation.why: This was explicitly covered in the session — the professor noted the 5-minute default during the monitoring configuration step.

questions.question: A team needs to deploy an updated version of their Elastic Beanstalk application with zero downtime. Which deployment policy is best?

options.text: All at once — it's the fastest
Rolling — no downtime, no extra instances
Immutable — new instances are created, tested, then old instances are terminated
Either B or C — both avoid downtime, the choice depends on rollback requirements

explanation.correct: Both Rolling and Immutable deployments achieve zero downtime. Immutable is safer (instant rollback by just terminating new instances) but costs more briefly. Rolling costs less but rollback requires a re-deploy.
explanation.why: All at once causes downtime. The best zero-downtime choice depends on whether you prioritize cost (Rolling) or rollback speed (Immutable).

questions.question: Which Elastic Beanstalk deployment strategy creates an entirely new set of instances, deploys the new version to them, and then terminates the old instances?

options.text: Rolling with additional batch
All at once
Immutable
In-place

explanation.correct: Immutable deployment creates a completely new Auto Scaling Group with new instances, deploys the new version there, and only after health checks pass does it terminate the old instances. This is the safest deployment strategy.
explanation.why: Rolling updates existing instances in batches. All at once updates everything simultaneously. Blue/Green is a separate CNAME swap approach.

questions.question: What is Blue/Green deployment in the context of Elastic Beanstalk?

options.text: Deploying to two availability zones simultaneously
Swapping the CNAME URLs of two environments to shift traffic instantly with no downtime
A color-coding system for environment health status
Deploying blue (stable) code while green (experimental) code is tested in Lambda

explanation.correct: Blue/Green deployment in Elastic Beanstalk means you maintain two identical environments. When ready, you swap their CNAME URLs — users instantly hit the new environment. Rollback is instant — swap back.
explanation.why: This allows zero-downtime releases and instant rollback without re-deploying code.

questions.question: A developer manually deletes the CloudFormation stack that Elastic Beanstalk created for an environment. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: Nothing — Elastic Beanstalk will recreate it automatically
The environment is cleanly terminated as expected
Resources may be left in an inconsistent state and the Beanstalk environment may become unmanageable
Only the EC2 instance is deleted; the rest of the environment remains

explanation.correct: You should NEVER manually delete the CloudFormation stack created by Elastic Beanstalk. Always terminate environments through the Beanstalk console. Manual stack deletion can leave resources in an inconsistent or zombie state.
explanation.why: Beanstalk manages the order of resource deletion carefully through CloudFormation. Bypassing this process causes issues.

questions.question: Which of the following accurately describes the relationship between Elastic Beanstalk environments and EC2 instances?

options.text: Each Elastic Beanstalk environment uses one shared EC2 instance across all applications
Elastic Beanstalk environments provision their own EC2 instances — visible in the EC2 console
Elastic Beanstalk uses Lambda functions instead of EC2 instances
EC2 instances created by Beanstalk are hidden and cannot be accessed in the EC2 console

explanation.correct: EC2 instances created by Elastic Beanstalk are fully visible in the EC2 console and are regular EC2 instances. You can SSH into them, modify their security groups, and see their metrics. They are tagged with the Beanstalk environment name.
explanation.why: Elastic Beanstalk is an orchestration layer — the underlying resources are real AWS resources, not abstracted away.

questions.question: A company has a Elastic Beanstalk application with three environments: Dev, Test, and Prod. The Dev team deploys a breaking change to Dev. How are Test and Prod affected?

options.text: All three environments update simultaneously
Test and Prod are automatically notified but not updated
Test and Prod are completely unaffected — each environment is independent
The deployment is blocked because it would break the other environments

explanation.correct: Each Elastic Beanstalk environment is completely independent. A deployment to Dev has no effect on Test or Prod. Each environment has its own EC2 instances, load balancer, and runs its own version of the application.
explanation.why: This is the key benefit of multiple environments — full isolation between development stages.

questions.question: Where does Elastic Beanstalk store uploaded application code versions?

options.text: In an EFS (Elastic File System) shared mount
Inside the EC2 instance's root volume only
In an Amazon S3 bucket automatically created by Elastic Beanstalk
In Amazon DynamoDB as binary data

explanation.correct: Elastic Beanstalk automatically creates an S3 bucket and stores all application code versions and logs there. This is why S3 buckets persist even after environment termination.
explanation.why: This S3 bucket is the source of truth for your application versions and must be manually deleted during cleanup.

questions.question: A startup wants to deploy a Node.js REST API that receives up to 10,000 requests/hour during business hours but almost none overnight. They want automatic scaling and minimal management. Which Elastic Beanstalk environment type fits best?

options.text: Single Instance — cheapest option
Worker Environment — for background processing
Load Balanced environment with Auto Scaling configured for business hours
Multi-container Docker environment

explanation.correct: A Load Balanced environment with Auto Scaling is ideal for variable traffic. Auto Scaling will add EC2 instances when traffic spikes and remove them when traffic drops, only charging for what is used.
explanation.why: Single instance cannot scale. Worker environments handle queue-based workloads, not HTTP requests. Multi-container Docker adds unnecessary complexity.

questions.question: A solutions architect needs to recommend a deployment approach for an application that currently runs on a specific custom AMI with a non-standard OS configuration. Should they use Elastic Beanstalk?

options.text: Yes — Elastic Beanstalk supports any custom AMI through the custom platform feature
No — Elastic Beanstalk only supports its own managed platforms and has limited AMI customization
Yes — just select the custom AMI option during environment creation
No — Elastic Beanstalk does not support EC2 at all

explanation.correct: Elastic Beanstalk does support custom platforms — you can build a custom AMI using Packer and use it as a Beanstalk platform. However, this adds complexity. For most cases, it is worth evaluating whether the custom AMI can be reproduced using Beanstalk's supported platforms with .ebextensions configuration files.
explanation.why: For highly customized infrastructure, EC2 with manual setup or ECS with a custom Docker image may be more appropriate than forcing the use of Beanstalk custom platforms.

questions.question: What is the purpose of .ebextensions configuration files in Elastic Beanstalk?

options.text: They define environment variables for the application
They allow customization of the environment — installing packages, running scripts, modifying configuration — as part of the deployment package
They are the application source code files
They configure the Elastic Load Balancer routing rules

explanation.correct: .ebextensions are YAML or JSON configuration files placed in a folder called .ebextensions in your application ZIP. They allow you to install OS packages, configure files, run commands, and modify AWS resource configurations during environment creation or deployment.
explanation.why: This is how you customize Elastic Beanstalk environments beyond the console UI options — for example, installing a custom library or configuring Nginx settings.

questions.question: An architect wants to ensure that if a new deployment to a production Elastic Beanstalk environment fails, traffic automatically continues to be served by the old version with no manual intervention. Which deployment policy satisfies this requirement?

options.text: All at once — fastest recovery
Rolling — reverts automatically on failure
Immutable — if new instances fail health checks, old instances are untouched and traffic continues
Rolling with additional batch — adds capacity before removing old instances

explanation.correct: Immutable deployment keeps the old instances completely untouched until the new instances pass all health checks. If the new deployment fails, the new instances are simply terminated and old instances continue serving traffic — zero manual intervention required.
explanation.why: Rolling updates old instances in-place, so a failure mid-deploy leaves some old and some broken instances. All at once causes downtime regardless.

questions.question: A company runs a Elastic Beanstalk web server environment. During peak hours, the CPU on the single EC2 instance hits 95%. What is the most operationally efficient way to handle this?

options.text: Manually SSH into the EC2 and upgrade the instance type
Delete the environment and recreate it with a larger instance type
Switch to a Load Balanced environment with Auto Scaling policies that scale out when CPU exceeds 70%
Add more Elastic Beanstalk applications to distribute load

explanation.correct: Converting to a Load Balanced environment and configuring Auto Scaling policies is the correct architectural solution. When CPU exceeds the threshold, Auto Scaling adds EC2 instances automatically; when load drops, they are terminated. This is the cloud-native, operationally efficient approach.
explanation.why: Manual SSH instance resizing is not scalable. Recreating the environment causes downtime. Multiple applications do not solve the problem of a single overloaded instance.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key difference between Elastic Beanstalk and AWS Lambda for deploying a web API?

options.text: Elastic Beanstalk supports more programming languages than Lambda
Lambda is always cheaper than Elastic Beanstalk regardless of traffic
Elastic Beanstalk runs on EC2 and can handle long-running connections and processes; Lambda is stateless with a 15-minute execution limit
Elastic Beanstalk does not support auto scaling; Lambda scales automatically

explanation.correct: Elastic Beanstalk runs your application on EC2 instances which can handle persistent connections, long-running processes, and stateful applications. Lambda functions are stateless and have a maximum execution time of 15 minutes, making them unsuitable for long-running workloads.
explanation.why: Lambda can be cheaper at low traffic volumes but is NOT always cheaper at high sustained traffic. Both services support auto scaling. Lambda has broader language support through custom runtimes.

questions.question: A developer terminates an Elastic Beanstalk environment but later notices CloudFormation still shows an associated stack in DELETE_FAILED state. What likely caused this?

options.text: The application still has code versions stored in the environment
A resource in the stack (e.g., an S3 bucket with objects) could not be deleted because it was not empty
The environment had more than one EC2 instance, which prevents stack deletion
Elastic Beanstalk requires a 24-hour cooling period before CloudFormation stacks can be deleted

explanation.correct: CloudFormation stack deletion fails most commonly when a resource cannot be deleted — typically an S3 bucket that still contains objects. CloudFormation cannot delete a non-empty S3 bucket. You must manually empty the bucket and then retry the stack deletion.
explanation.why: This is a common real-world issue when cleaning up Elastic Beanstalk environments.

questions.question: Your Elastic Beanstalk application needs to connect to an RDS database. What is the recommended approach for passing database credentials securely?

options.text: Hard-code the database URL and password directly in the application source code
Use Elastic Beanstalk environment variables to pass DB_HOST, DB_USER, and DB_PASSWORD — these are encrypted at rest
Store credentials in a plaintext .env file uploaded with the application ZIP
Email the credentials to all developers so they can configure it manually

explanation.correct: Elastic Beanstalk environment variables are the recommended way to pass configuration like database credentials. They are accessible to the application at runtime and are not stored in the source code. For production workloads, AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store provides even stronger security.
explanation.why: Hard-coding credentials in source code or config files is a serious security risk, especially when code is stored in version control.

questions.question: A team is migrating from Heroku to AWS and wants the closest equivalent experience. Which AWS service most closely mirrors the Heroku 'git push to deploy' experience?

options.text: Amazon EC2 with CodeDeploy
AWS Elastic Beanstalk with the EB CLI
Amazon ECS with Fargate
AWS CodePipeline alone

explanation.correct: Elastic Beanstalk is the closest AWS equivalent to Heroku. The EB CLI allows 'eb deploy' to push code directly, similar to Heroku's git push workflow. Both are PaaS solutions where the platform manages infrastructure.
explanation.why: EC2+CodeDeploy requires more manual setup. ECS requires container knowledge. CodePipeline is a CI/CD service, not a PaaS.

questions.question: What happens to the RDS database if you terminate an Elastic Beanstalk environment that has an integrated RDS instance (created through Beanstalk)?

options.text: The RDS instance is always preserved regardless of termination settings
The RDS instance is deleted along with the environment by default, but you can configure it to be retained
The RDS instance is automatically migrated to another environment
The RDS instance becomes a standalone RDS instance automatically

explanation.correct: When you terminate an Elastic Beanstalk environment that contains an integrated RDS instance, the RDS instance is deleted by default. You can configure a 'deletion policy' to retain the database — which creates a final snapshot and keeps the database alive after the environment is gone.
explanation.why: This is a critical consideration for production environments. Never use Beanstalk-integrated RDS for production databases — instead, create RDS separately and connect via environment variables, so database lifecycle is independent of environment lifecycle.

questions.question: An exam question states: 'A developer wants to deploy an application to AWS and retain full control over the operating system, middleware, and runtime, while also having AWS manage infrastructure provisioning.' Which service best matches?

options.text: AWS Lambda — serverless, no OS control needed
AWS Elastic Beanstalk — PaaS with configurable underlying OS and runtime access
Amazon ECS with Fargate — container-based, no OS management
AWS App Runner — fully managed, no OS access

explanation.correct: Elastic Beanstalk is the answer when the requirement is: (1) AWS manages infrastructure provisioning AND (2) developer retains access to OS, middleware, and configuration. You can SSH into Beanstalk EC2 instances, use .ebextensions to customize the OS, and modify any underlying resource.
explanation.why: Lambda and Fargate abstract away the OS entirely. App Runner provides even less control. Only Beanstalk gives PaaS convenience with EC2-level access when needed.
